bioghist.head: Biographical note
bioghist.p: John Pope was born around 1857 to Bavarian parents who had immigrated to the United States. He started working as a clerk at a tobacco company, and by age 23 he was boarding with the Arents family. Pope soon acquired his own fortune in the tobacco industry, but he died in 1896. His money was divided among friends and family, including George Arents, his brother George P. Pope, and his sisters Kunigunde Mullin, Margaret Pope, and Eva Kreiser. The Bushwick property was deeded to all four siblings, and the sisters let their younger brother George handle their combined finances. He had a pipe organ built in the house and bought chandeliers, fine rugs, music boxes, pianos, and stained glass windows. The photographs even show a white peacock in the backyard. George Pope was a faithful Catholic and gave generously to local churches, providing the marble altar at the Church of St. John the Baptist on Willoughby Avenue as well as the organ at St. Barbara's. He also donated funds to Catholic charities, and was recognized by Pope Leo XIII with the Order of St. Gregory the Great in 1902.

George's sister Kunigunde, who had been widowed, became concerned that her children would not have the inheritance to which they were entitled due to her brother's spending. She sued George and in 1909 the siblings reached an agreement, at which time the house and its contents were valued at $2 million. Soon thereafter, Mrs. Mullin had moved with her son to 74 Woodruff Avenue in Flatbush. George passed away in 1917 and the mansion was sold in 1920 to the Jewish Home for the Aged and Infirm (later known as the Menorah Home) for just $150,000. In the 1950s, the mansion was demolished by the Menorah Home to be replaced with a more modern building.
